correctness.rationale: For every positive distance, dispersion and pulse duration with nonnegative drift, the derivative sign reduces to the sign of a shifted-density logarithmic ratio. That ratio has derivative numerator a quadratic with one positive zero, starts at +infinity and ends negative or at zero from below. Thus it crosses zero once, giving a strict global post-shutoff peak. The shifted density crosses its unimodal mode, making the implicit derivatives well defined and strict. The derived positive-root equation yields the two fixed-drift asymptotics and the uniform scaled crossover without invoking finite enumeration; the standard-library script tests independent numerical instances and records its non-proof limitations.

originality.rationale: The kernel and its integration over release times are prior knowledge. The specific claim is a sharp characterization of the maximum of a finite-duration first-passage flux, its strict parameter sensitivities, and a singular drift-dependent long-release asymptotic including the scaling transition. No inspected whole primary work or record had the same assumptions and implication. An older relevant moment method for step inputs and original dispersion article were not accessible in full, so exact historical priority is not claimed.
residual_risks: The archived Yu–Warrick–Conklin step-input paper and Kreft–Zuber transport derivation were inaccessible as complete texts, so stronger mathematical coverage is not excluded.
A general theorem on shifted inverse-Gaussian profiles or translated unimodal densities may already imply part of the classification or asymptotics.
The distinction between absorbing first-passage flux and resident downstream concentration is essential; extending claims across that distinction would be incorrect.

value.rationale: Finite-duration contaminant-release response at an absorbing receiver is a natural hydrological transport observable. The theorem determines whether maximum loading occurs after source termination, bounds how lag reacts to added drift and release length, and finds two asymptotically incompatible lag scales and their transition. The cross-regime law and global monotonicity are more than a normalization identity or a routine numerical peak; they are useful for differentiating no-drift and advective pulse monitoring scenarios, with exact model limits stated.
